pedagogy.summary: The benchmark fractions 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 have decimal names — 0.5, 0.25, 0.75 — that should be understood, not merely memorised, by routing through hundredths: 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25, because a quarter of a hundred squares is 25 of them. Grounding the equivalence in an equivalent-fraction step on a hundred square (or a number line where 1/4 and 0.25 mark the same point) prevents the digit-copying error that treats 1/4 as '0.14' or '0.4'. These three equivalents are high-utility landmarks for the whole fraction–decimal–percentage web, so the priority is that children can both recall them and explain WHY they hold.
bestPractices: Derive each equivalent through hundredths on a 10×10 grid: 1/4 of 100 squares = 25 squares = 25/100 = 0.25; 1/2 = 50/100 = 0.5; 3/4 = 75/100 = 0.75.
Use a number line to show 1/4 and 0.25 landing on the SAME point, reinforcing that the fraction and decimal name one value.
Contrast the correct route with the digit-copying trap: 1/4 is NOT 0.14 or 0.4 — check by shading a quarter of the grid (25 squares, not 4).
Build the three as a connected family (1/4, 1/2, 3/4 ↔ 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) and connect to money (£ and quarters) and measures for familiar anchors.
Move both directions — fraction to decimal and decimal to fraction — and ask children to justify with the grid, so recall is backed by reasoning.
keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundred grid with a quarter (25 squares), half (50), three-quarters (75) shaded
Number line where 1/4 and 0.25 share a point (also 1/2 = 0.5, 3/4 = 0.75)
Fraction↔decimal matching cards for the three landmarks
commonMisconceptions: Digit-copying: writing 1/4 as 0.14 or 0.4 (treating numerator/denominator digits as decimal digits).
Denominator-as-count on the grid: shading 4 squares for 1/4 (reading 1/4 as 4/100 = 0.04).
Believing 0.25 > 0.5 because '25 > 5' (whole-number bias across the decimal).
Treating the fraction and its decimal as different, unrelated values.
Recalling the facts with no grounding, so errors cannot be self-checked.

learn.summary: Children should learn the benchmark decimal names for 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 (0.5, 0.25, 0.75) by understanding WHY they hold, not just memorising them. The reliable route is through hundredths: 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25 because a quarter of a hundred squares is 25 of them. Grounding this on a 10×10 grid (and a number line where 1/4 and 0.25 mark the same point) helps counter the digit-copying error (1/4 → '0.14' or '0.4') and the denominator-as-count error (shading 4 squares). These three equivalents are high-utility landmarks across the fraction–decimal–percentage web, so children should be able to both recall them and justify them.

activities.title: Shade a quarter: finding 0.25 on the hundred grid
feedback: If a learner shades 4 squares for 1/4, point out that a quarter means splitting the whole into FOUR equal groups and taking one group; count that group (25 squares), not four single squares.

If a learner writes 1/4 as 0.4, have them shade what 0.4 would be (40 squares) and compare to a shaded quarter (25 squares): 40 is far more than a quarter, so 0.4 cannot be 1/4; the correct name is 0.25.
If a learner writes 1/4 as 0.14, show that the digits of the fraction are not simply copied into the decimal; route through 25/100 to reach 0.25.
When correct, prompt: 'A quarter is 25 of the 100 — how many is a half? And three-quarters? Show it.'
activities.rationale: Shading a fraction of a hundred grid makes the count of squares and the decimal emerge together, grounding the equivalence in place value and equivalent fractions rather than digit manipulation. Testing a wrong guess (0.4 → 40 squares) lets the child see why digit-copying fails. A linked number line reinforces 'same value, two names'.
sourceClaims: Some fractions are easily converted to decimals, and this equivalence is built by converting to a fraction with denominator 100 (e.g. via a hundred square); the hundred square, fraction with denominator 100, decimal and number line are recommended parallel representations for these equivalents.
learnerActions: On a 10×10 grid of 100 squares, split the whole into four equal groups and shade one group to make a quarter.
Count the shaded squares (25) and write the result as 25/100, then as the decimal 0.25.
Repeat for one half (50 squares = 50/100 = 0.5) and three-quarters (75 squares = 75/100 = 0.75), building the three as a connected family.
Mark 1/4 and 0.25 on a number line and check they land on the SAME point; do the same for 1/2 = 0.5 and 3/4 = 0.75.
Work in both directions: given a fraction, find the decimal; given the decimal, shade the grid and name the fraction, justifying each with the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter of 100 is 25 squares, so 1/4 and 0.25 name one and the same value — a fact the child can rebuild for 1/2 and 3/4 rather than recall blindly.

activities.title: Predict, then check: why isn't a quarter 4 squares?
feedback: A prediction of '4 because of the 4 in 1/4' signals reading the denominator as a number of squares; correct by splitting into four equal groups of 25 and taking one group.
If the prediction was 25, ask the child to articulate the rule: each quarter is 100 ÷ 4 = 25 squares.
After reconciling, ask the child to predict for 3/4 and check (three groups of 25 = 75).
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check routine turns a hidden misconception into a visible, discussable moment and gives the child ownership of the correction. Reading a fraction as two independent whole numbers (the denominator as a count) is a documented error source best countered with area and place-value models such as the grid used here.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a fraction as two independent whole numbers, or judging a decimal by the size of its digits — is a central, documented source of error and must be countered with place-value and area models.
learnerActions: Before shading anything, predict how many of the 100 squares you will shade for 1/4, and say WHY.
Then shade a quarter by splitting into four equal groups and taking one; count the squares.
Reconcile the count (25) with your prediction: if you predicted 4, explain what went wrong.
Read off 25/100 = 0.25 and state whether 1/4 and 0.25 are the same value or different.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the prediction explicit surfaces the denominator-as-count error ('4, because of the 4 in 1/4') so the child confronts and corrects it against the actual 25 squares.

activities.title: Which is bigger: 0.25 or 0.5?
feedback: If a learner says 0.25 > 0.5 because 25 > 5, show that 0.5 covers 50 squares and 0.25 covers only 25, so 0.5 is larger; compare tenths first (5 tenths vs 2 tenths).
Reinforce that 0.5 and 0.50 name the same value (50 of 100 squares) to settle the comparison.
activities.rationale: Direct comparison on area models counters whole-number bias across the decimal point, a known persistent error, by making the relative sizes visible.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a fraction as two independent whole numbers, or judging a decimal by the size of its digits — is a central, documented source of error and must be countered with place-value and area models.
learnerActions: Shade a quarter (25 squares) and a half (50 squares) on separate hundred grids and compare the shaded areas.
Decide which decimal is larger, 0.25 or 0.5, and explain the choice using the grids rather than the digit strings.
State why '25 is more than 5' does not make 0.25 bigger, referring to tenths and hundredths place value.
Order 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 and check the order against the grids and the number line.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing decimals means comparing by highest place value (tenths first), not by treating the digits after the point as whole numbers; a quarter is clearly less than a half on the grid.

activities.title: Connect to money and matching
feedback: If matching relies on guessing, ask the child to justify each pair via the grid or the £1 = 100p anchor.
Recall without justification ('I just know 1/4 is 0.25') is partial: prompt for the 25/100 reasoning so the fact can be self-checked.
If transfer to a new fraction stalls, return to 'how many of 100 squares?' as the anchoring question.
activities.rationale: The fill-in hundredths chain (1/4 = __/100 = 0.__) applies the denominator-100 representation the source recommends and extends to other fractions whose denominators divide 100 exactly. Money and measures add familiar anchors (not drawn from the cited source), and bidirectional matching backed by justification keeps recall grounded in reasoning rather than isolated facts.
sourceClaims: Some fractions are easily converted to decimals, and this equivalence is built by converting to a fraction with denominator 100 (e.g. via a hundred square); the hundred square, fraction with denominator 100, decimal and number line are recommended parallel representations for these equivalents.
learnerActions: Fill in the hundredths chain for each landmark: 1/4 = __/100 = 0.__, 1/2 = __/100 = 0.__, 3/4 = __/100 = 0.__, justifying the denominator-100 step.
Link each equivalent to money as a familiar anchor: £1 = 100p, so a quarter = 25p = £0.25, a half = 50p = £0.50, three-quarters = 75p = £0.75.
Match fraction cards to decimal cards for the three landmarks (1/4↔0.25, 1/2↔0.5, 3/4↔0.75).

Transfer the hundredths route to a new fraction whose denominator divides 100 exactly (for example 1/5 = 20/100 = 0.2 or 1/10 = 10/100 = 0.1), explaining how many of the 100 squares it covers, just as you did for a quarter.
activities.intendedInsight: The three equivalents form a reusable family: the denominator-100 route extends to other fractions whose denominators divide 100 exactly (such as tenths, fifths and twentieths), and familiar contexts like money give extra anchors for recall.

constraints: Target learners are roughly ages 8–9; this is conceptual work on recognising and writing decimal equivalents of 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4. The Year 4 statutory expectation to recognise and write these decimal equivalents is the curriculum anchor (its source was flagged unverified).
Insist that recall is backed by the 25/100 reasoning: a child who recalls 1/4 = 0.25 but cannot justify it on the grid, or grounds one landmark but not the family, has only partial understanding.

A static reference card showing the three shadings with labels is useful for review, but on its own it does not let a child shade, predict, or test wrong answers; use it as a reference scaffold alongside active shading, not as a replacement for it.

Recognition and matching tasks check whether the facts are known and can diagnose digit-copying (0.4/0.14 distractors) and denominator-as-count, but they do not by themselves build the grid-grounded reasoning or elicit the child's own justification.

An interactive grid that recolours as the child shades, counts squares, and shows the linked number-line point is one effective way to make the mechanism concrete, but it is an example, not a required tool; paper hundred grids and a drawn number line serve the same purpose.
Distinguish the mathematical idea (a value named two ways) from any particular display: the number-line point and the grid are representations of the same single value.

The source asserted that the grid approach 'directly defeats' the misconceptions and that a conversation 'adds nothing' and 3D 'adds no value'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established comparative-efficacy findings; they have been softened to scoped proposals and omitted as universal claims.
Money and measures anchors are retained from the original pedagogy but are not supported by any cited source claim; the hundredths chain is the source-backed element of the final activity.

Arithmetic checked: 1/4 of 100 = 25; 1/2 = 50; 3/4 = 75; 0.4 of 100 = 40 squares; 100 ÷ 4 = 25. The comparison 0.5 > 0.25 (5 tenths vs 2 tenths) is correct. No arithmetic errors found in the migrated content.
The reteach prerequisite identifiers from the source (equivalent-fractions and place-value prerequisites) are referenced conceptually in feedback but internal IDs have been removed.

assess.poeTask: Before shading, ask the child to PREDICT how many of the 100 squares they will shade for 1/4 — some say 4, some say 25 — and to say WHY. The reason is diagnostic: '4, because of the 4 in 1/4' reveals denominator-as-count. Then shade a quarter (split into four equal groups, take one) and count 25. Have the child reconcile the 25 with their prediction and read off 25/100 = 0.25.
probeDeeper: You shaded a quarter and got 25 squares. How many squares is a half, and what decimal is that?
Is 1/4 the same value as 0.25, or are they different because one is a fraction and one is a decimal?
Which is bigger, 0.25 or 0.5 — and why, when 25 is more than 5?
What is 3/4 as a decimal? Show it on the grid — how many squares, and how did you get there from a quarter?
assess.correctAnswer: 1/4 = 0.25. On the grid, a quarter of the 100 squares is 25 squares, so 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25.

errorPatterns.pattern: Digit-copying: writes 1/4 as 0.14 or 0.4, treating the fraction's digits as decimal digits (fraction as two separate whole numbers).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Route through hundredths: 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25; shade a quarter and count 25 squares. Reteach equivalent fractions so the fraction is seen as one value, not two digits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 0.4 or 0.14 for 1/4; on the grid cannot justify it (0.4 would be 40 squares, not a quarter).

errorPatterns.pattern: Denominator-as-count: shades 4 squares for 1/4 (reads 1/4 as 4 out of 100 = 0.04).
errorPatterns.nextMove: A quarter of 100 squares is found by splitting into 4 equal groups of 25, not by taking 4 squares; shade one group. Reteach equivalent fractions (1/4 = 25/100).
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/4 of the hundred grid is 4 squares.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shades 4 squares on the grid and/or gives 0.04; treats the denominator as a number of squares.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias across the decimal: believes 0.25 > 0.5 because '25 is more than 5'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the grid, a quarter (25 squares) is clearly less than a half (50 squares); compare by highest place value. Reteach place value of tenths/hundredths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a probe, orders 0.25 above 0.5; compares the decimal tails as whole numbers.

responseLevels.gap: Digit-copies (1/4 → 0.14/0.4) or shades 4 squares; cannot connect 1/4 to 25/100. Treats fraction and decimal as unrelated.
responseLevels.full: States 1/4 = 0.25 and explains it as 25/100 by shading a quarter (25 of 100 squares), extends the reasoning to 1/2 = 0.5 and 3/4 = 0.75, treats fraction and decimal as one value on a number line, and transfers the hundredths route to a new benchmark fraction.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls 1/4 = 0.25 (and often 1/2, 3/4) but cannot justify it on the grid, or grounds one but not the family — knows the facts without the 25/100 reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 1/4 as a decimal. Then use this 10×10 grid to explain WHY it equals that decimal.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The decimal alone can be recalled or guessed; the grid explanation separates a child who grounds 1/4 in 25/100 from one who digit-copies (0.14, 0.4) or shades 4 squares (denominator-as-count). A child reasoning correctly shades 25 squares and reads 25/100; the common errors produce a different, self-revealing picture.
